newsitem.title: USA: U.S. congratulates French left on election victory.
newsitem.headline: U.S. congratulates French left on election victory.

text.p: The United States on Sunday congratulated France's Socialist Party on its election victory, with government officials and academic experts predicting little change in U.S.-French relations.
"The United States congratulates the Socialist Party and its allies on their clear victory," said State Department spokesman Julie Reside.
"We look forward to the naming of the new prime minister and cabinet. As always, we welcome the opportunity to continue our close cooperation with France," she said.
Reside said U.S. relations with France had always been excellent and she expected U.S.-French relations to remain close and cooperative under the new left-wing government.

French government sources said Prime Minister Alain Juppe would tender his resignation to President Jacques Chirac on Monday morning following Sunday's election defeat and Socialist leader Lionel Jospin should be appointed to succeed him immediately.
The Clinton administration says its relations with Paris are good, and that it admires Chirac, who once worked at a Howard Johnson restaurant in the United States.
But ties have been troubled in recent years by a series of disputes relating to NATO, Africa and other international issues.

Prof. Robert Lieber, chairman of the Department of Government at Georgetown University, said he expected no significant change in U.S.-French relations, noting that foreign policy was largely the domain of the French president, not the parliamentary majority.

He attributed the defeat of the ruling conservatives to France's economic malaise and its 12-percent unemployment rate -- the highest among the Group of Seven industrialised countries -- adding, "It's not surprising that the government of the day paid the political price."
Harvey Feigenbaum, a professor of political science at George Washington University, agreed that similar factors had led to the defeat of the Socialists four years ago.
"The reality is that U.S.-French relations are not going to change very much," he said. "Those kind of things that were sticking points will stay sticking points."

For instance, Washington has strongly resisted a push by France to have a European take over NATO's Naples-based Southern Command (AFSOUTH), which has hitherto always been held by an American. The two countries also clashed this week at a NATO meeting in Portugal over which new members should be admitted to the alliance.
Reside said the United States would revisit the Southern Command issue with the new French government once it was in place.
